html:
Mohenjo-daro, on the Indus river in Sindh, Pakistan, was built around 2600 to 2500 BCE and became one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley civilisation and one of the world's earliest major cities. Its name, given much later in Sindhi, means "mound of the dead men".

It probably held at least 40,000 people. The city had two parts. A raised western mound held big public buildings, including the Great Bath, a brick-lined, waterproofed pool that may have been used for ritual washing. A larger lower town spread out on a grid of streets, with brick houses built around courtyards, many with their own wells and bathrooms draining into covered sewers.

Finds from the site include the bronze Dancing Girl, the stone "priest-king" bust and many seals carved with animals and signs of the Indus script. Like the other Indus cities it was a contemporary of the pyramids of Old Kingdom Egypt and of the cities of Sumer.

Mohenjo-daro was abandoned by about 1700 BCE, as the Indus cities declined. It was rediscovered in the 1920s, when R. D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India began excavating it. Since 1980 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and salt and the rising water table now threaten its bricks.
